qs.q: The Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) controls vector populations by
o: Using pheromones to confuse mating behavior
Releasing sterilized males that mate unsuccessfully with wild females
Introducing predators that eat the vectors
qs.e: SIT involves mass-rearing vectors, sterilizing males (usually with radiation), and releasing them. When sterile males mate with wild females, no offspring are produced, leading to population decline over generations.

ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: The Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) releases radiation‑sterilized male insects to mate with wild females, yielding no viable offspring and gradually suppressing disease‑vector populations.

sections.p: SIT is a biological control method that reduces populations of disease‑transmitting insects, chiefly mosquitoes, by flooding the environment with sterile males.
b: Targets reproductive capacity, not adult survival
Works best when the target species is isolated and has limited migration

sections.p: Mosquitoes (e.g., Aedes aegypti, Anopheles spp.) are small, dipteran insects with aquatic larvae and adult females that bite humans to obtain blood for egg development.
b: Females require a blood meal for oogenesis
Males do not bite and can be mass‑reared in insectaries

sections.p: Adult females lay eggs on water surfaces; larvae develop through four instars before emerging as adults. Pathogens are acquired during blood meals and transmitted when infected females bite.
b: Larval habitats: stagnant water, containers, rice fields
Adult lifespan: 2‑4 weeks, longer in cooler climates

sections.p: Mosquitoes are vectors for malaria, dengue, Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever and filarial infections, all of which cause significant morbidity in low‑resource settings.
b: Malaria: cyclic fever, anemia, cerebral involvement

sections.p: Clinical diagnosis of vector‑borne disease relies on history of exposure, symptom pattern and specific laboratory tests; SIT itself is evaluated by entomological surveillance.
b: Rapid diagnostic tests for malaria antigens
Mosquito trap counts to assess SIT impact

t.b: What is the current vector population? Low counts indicate successful SIT; high counts suggest need for program adjustment
Are released males effectively sterilized? >95% sterility confirms radiation dose adequacy
Is the patient infected? Positive result guides treatment; negative result prompts alternative diagnoses

sections.p: SIT is a control measure, not a therapy. Clinical management of vector‑borne disease follows standard protocols; SIT complements insecticide spraying, environmental management and personal protection.
b: Treat malaria with artemisinin‑based combination therapy
Manage dengue with fluid resuscitation and monitoring
Use diethylcarbamazine for filariasis after confirming infection

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams:
b: SIT reduces vector numbers by producing no viable offspring
Effective when released males outnumber wild males by >10:1
Success measured by sustained drop in trap counts and disease incidence

whenToSeekHelp: High fever with altered mental status (possible cerebral malaria)
Severe abdominal pain and vomiting with dengue warning signs (plasma leakage)
Rapidly progressive limb swelling and skin changes (filariasis complications)

faq.q: Why are only male insects released in SIT?
faq.a: Males do not bite, so they pose no disease risk, and they compete with wild males for mates, maximizing sterility impact.
SIT reduces reliance on chemicals but is usually combined with other measures for rapid control.

faq.q: What happens if sterile males are released in an area with high mosquito migration?
faq.a: Immigration of fertile females can dilute the effect; border control or larger release zones are needed.
